explanations.explanation: Job says, "If only I knew where to find Him, so that I could go to His seat." (Job 23:3) He's hurting, and his biggest wish is still to find God. I think that tells you where Job's heart is pointing. When life gets heavy, he wants God in the room.

Job doesn't wish for anything about his friends in this verse. His friends have done plenty of talking, but Job's wish goes past them. He says, "If only I knew where to find Him…" (Job 23:3). The one he's looking for is God.

explanations.answer: How long his pain will last
explanations.explanation: Job's pain is real. He calls his complaint bitter and says God's hand is heavy (Job 23:2). But he never asks for a countdown. His wish is to know where to find God, so he could go to His seat (Job 23:3). I'd have been asking for a timer, honestly.

Job wants a real conversation, and that includes listening. He says, "I would learn how He would answer, and consider what He would say." (Job 23:5) So this one is False. Job plans to speak, but he also wants to hear God's answer.

That's right. Job wants more than a speech. He says, "I would learn how He would answer, and consider what He would say." (Job 23:5) He's ready to listen, which tells you he wants an actual answer and not just a chance to vent.

Job says, "No, He would certainly take note of me." (Job 23:6) He wonders if God would contend with him in great power, and then he answers his own question. He believes God would pay attention to him. That's a lot of hope from a man in this much pain.

Job says the opposite here. He asks if God would contend with him in His great power. Then he answers, "No, He would certainly take note of me." (Job 23:6) Job pictures God noticing him, not looking away.

Job isn't picturing that. He asks, "Would He contend with me in His great power?" and then answers, "No, He would certainly take note of me." (Job 23:6) In Job's picture, God pays attention to him and doesn't strike him.

Job says, "I would be delivered forever from my Judge." (Job 23:7) He calls God his Judge here. He pictures an upright man reasoning with Him and walking away set free. That's the outcome Job is hoping for.

Job pictures the opposite ending. He says an upright man could reason with God, "and I would be delivered forever from my Judge." (Job 23:7) Delivered means set free. Job isn't expecting a guilty verdict in this picture.

Job isn't asking to be forgotten. He wants God to notice him, because he says God "would certainly take note of me." (Job 23:6) Then he says he would be "delivered forever from my Judge." (Job 23:7) Delivered is the word.
Job says, "Yet He knows the way I have taken." (Job 23:10) He can't see God anywhere, but he's sure God sees him. That one little "yet" carries a lot of weight. I think Job is holding on to it.
Job doesn't say anything about his friends' plans here. After saying he can't find God in any direction, he says, "Yet He knows the way I have taken." (Job 23:10) What God knows is Job's own path.

Job doesn't mention that here. He's just said he can't find God in any direction. Then comes the turn: "Yet He knows the way I have taken." (Job 23:10) God knows Job's path, even when Job can't see God.

Job says, "when He has tested me, I will come forth as gold." (Job 23:10) He's in the middle of the testing, and he still expects to come out of it as gold. That's a bold thing to say from where he's sitting.
Dust is where I spent a lot of years, so I know it well. It's not what Job says, though. He says, "I will come forth as gold." (Job 23:10) Gold is the word he picked.
Job doesn't say ashes here. He says that when God has tested him, "I will come forth as gold." (Job 23:10) He expects to come out of the testing as something valuable.

Job says, "I have not departed from the command of His lips." (Job 23:12) Then he adds that he has treasured the words of God's mouth more than his daily bread. For a man this hungry for answers, that's a big claim. God's words come first, even before bread.

Job says no such thing. His friends have had plenty of counsel for him, but here he talks about God. He says, "I have not departed from the command of His lips." (Job 23:12) The command he's following is God's.

Job doesn't mention land here. He says, "I have not departed from the command of His lips; I have treasured the words of His mouth more than my daily bread." (Job 23:12) It's God's words he's holding on to.

Job says, "For He carries out His decree against me, and He has many such plans." (Job 23:14) The mood is heavy here. Job feels that what he's facing may not be the only thing God has planned. It's no wonder fear comes next.

The text says it. Job says, "For He carries out His decree against me, and He has many such plans." (Job 23:14) So this one is True. Job believes there are many more plans like it, and that's why he's afraid.

Job says, "Therefore I am terrified in His presence; when I consider this, I fear Him." (Job 23:15) He just said God is unchangeable and does what He desires. Thinking it over, Job is afraid. He says it plainly, with no sugarcoating.

Job isn't feeling peaceful in this moment. He says, "Therefore I am terrified in His presence; when I consider this, I fear Him." (Job 23:15) Thinking about a God who does what He desires leaves him afraid.
Job doesn't say he feels welcome. He says, "Therefore I am terrified in His presence." (Job 23:15) The more he thinks about it, the more he fears. It's honest, and it's heavy.

Job says the opposite. After talking about thick darkness, he says, "Yet I am not silenced by the darkness, by the thick darkness that covers my face." (Job 23:17) So this one is False. The darkness is real, but it doesn't shut Job up.

That's right. Job says, "Yet I am not silenced by the darkness, by the thick darkness that covers my face." (Job 23:17) His heart is faint and he's afraid, but he keeps talking. That little "yet" shows up again.

Job says, "Men move boundary stones; they pasture stolen flocks." (Job 24:2) Boundary stones marked where one person's land ended. Moving them is a quiet way to take what isn't yours. It's the first thing on Job's list.
Idols aren't on Job's list here. He starts with this: "Men move boundary stones; they pasture stolen flocks." (Job 24:2) He's talking about taking land and animals that belong to other people.

That's not what Job lists first. He says, "Men move boundary stones; they pasture stolen flocks." (Job 24:2) The first wrong he names is moving a boundary marker, and stealing flocks comes right behind it.

Job says, "They push the needy off the road and force all the poor of the land into hiding." (Job 24:4) The poor aren't just struggling. They're being pushed out of sight. Job is laying out what he sees.

The text says it plainly. Job says, "They push the needy off the road and force all the poor of the land into hiding." (Job 24:4) So this one is True. The poor are pushed off the road and into hiding.
Job says, "Drenched by mountain rains, they huddle against the rocks for want of shelter." (Job 24:8) No roof, so a rock is the wall they've got. I think this one hurts to picture.

Job doesn't put them in a city gate. He says, "Drenched by mountain rains, they huddle against the rocks for want of shelter." (Job 24:8) They have no shelter at all, so rocks are all they have to lean on.
No tree shows up in this verse. Job says, "Drenched by mountain rains, they huddle against the rocks for want of shelter." (Job 24:8) Cold rain, bare rock, and nowhere else to go.

explanations.answer: They still go hungry and thirsty
explanations.explanation: Job says, "They carry the sheaves, but still go hungry." (Job 24:10) Then he says they tread the winepresses "but go thirsty." (Job 24:11) They do the work, and the harvest doesn't feed them. I think this one is heavy, and it's okay to feel it.

explanations.answer: They get a share of the harvest
explanations.explanation: Job says the opposite. "They carry the sheaves, but still go hungry." (Job 24:10) They work right next to the harvest and still go without. That's what troubles Job.

explanations.answer: They earn a house in the city
explanations.explanation: Job never mentions a house for them. He says they carry the sheaves "but still go hungry," and tread the winepresses "but go thirsty." (Job 24:10-11) Their work doesn't bring them what they need.

Job says, "From the city, men groan, and the souls of the wounded cry out, yet God charges no one with wrongdoing." (Job 24:12) The cries are loud, and Job doesn't see anyone being charged. That's his complaint.

Job doesn't say that God charges the poor. He says the wounded cry out, "yet God charges no one with wrongdoing." (Job 24:12) His complaint is that no one is charged at all, even with all that groaning.
That's what Job is wondering about. He says, "yet God charges no one with wrongdoing." (Job 24:12) The word is no one, and Job doesn't see anyone being charged, even while the wounded cry out.

Job says, "When daylight is gone, the murderer rises to kill the poor and needy; in the night he is like a thief." (Job 24:14) This is a dark verse, and Job doesn't soften it. He's naming the harm done to the poor and needy.
Job doesn't use a lion here. He says, "in the night he is like a thief." (Job 24:14) It's a heavy verse about killing the poor and needy, and the picture is someone sneaking in the dark.
Job doesn't say wolf. He says the murderer rises when daylight is gone, and "in the night he is like a thief." (Job 24:14) It's a heavy verse, and the picture is a thief in the dark.
Job says the opposite. Of those who dig through houses in the dark, he says, "by day they shut themselves in, never to experience the light." (Job 24:16) So this one is False. They stay hidden away.

That's right. Job says, "In the dark they dig through houses; by day they shut themselves in, never to experience the light." (Job 24:16) They stay hidden during the day and don't come out into the light.

Job says, "their portion of the land is cursed, so that no one turns toward their vineyards." (Job 24:18) Their land is cursed, and nobody even looks toward their vineyards. That's quite a picture next to "foam on the surface of the water."
Job says the reverse. "Their portion of the land is cursed, so that no one turns toward their vineyards." (Job 24:18) Nobody turns toward their vineyards, which is a long way from fruitful.

Stolen isn't the word Job uses for their land here. He says, "their portion of the land is cursed, so that no one turns toward their vineyards." (Job 24:18) Cursed is the word, and nobody looks their way.

Job says, "As drought and heat consume the melting snow, so Sheol steals those who have sinned." (Job 24:19) Sheol is the place of the dead. Snow doesn't stand a chance against drought and heat, and that's the picture Job uses.

That's not the comparison Job makes. He says, "As drought and heat consume the melting snow, so Sheol steals those who have sinned." (Job 24:19) Sheol is the place of the dead, and the picture is snow vanishing in the heat.
Job doesn't use fire and thorns here. He says, "As drought and heat consume the melting snow, so Sheol steals those who have sinned." (Job 24:19) It's snow disappearing in drought and heat.

Job says, "The womb forgets them; the worm feeds on them; they are remembered no more." (Job 24:20) It's a sober line about where those who have sinned end up. Job is not cheering here. He's describing what he says happens.
The text says it directly. Job says, "The womb forgets them; the worm feeds on them; they are remembered no more." (Job 24:20) So this one is True. Job says they are remembered no more.

explanations.answer: His eyes are on their ways
explanations.explanation: Job says, "He gives them a sense of security, but His eyes are on their ways." (Job 24:23) The mighty may feel safe. God is still watching every step. Feeling secure and being secure are two different things.

explanations.answer: His face is hidden from them
explanations.explanation: Job says the opposite. "He gives them a sense of security, but His eyes are on their ways." (Job 24:23) God's eyes are on them, so they aren't hidden from Him at all.

Job doesn't say that. He says God drags away the mighty, and "they have no assurance of life." (Job 24:22) Then he adds that God gives them a sense of security, "but His eyes are on their ways." (Job 24:23) Their feeling of safety doesn't last forever.
Job says, "They are exalted for a moment, then they are gone." (Job 24:24) A moment is short. The mighty may look high up, but it doesn't last. They are brought low like all others.
Job picks a much shorter word. He says, "They are exalted for a moment, then they are gone." (Job 24:24) A lifetime is long, and a moment is not.
That's far too long for what Job says. He says, "They are exalted for a moment, then they are gone." (Job 24:24) A moment is the word, and the mighty are gone fast.
Job says, "If this is not so, then who can prove me a liar and reduce my words to nothing?" (Job 24:25) He's standing behind everything he just said. He's daring anyone to show him wrong.
Job doesn't ask anyone to find God for him. His wish to find God came earlier (Job 23:3). Here he ends with a challenge: "who can prove me a liar and reduce my words to nothing?" (Job 24:25)
Job isn't asking for court here. He did talk about pleading his case before God (Job 23:4). His closing challenge is this: "who can prove me a liar and reduce my words to nothing?" (Job 24:25)
